They will come to know.﴾ ﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle,﴾ ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ ﴿And We created you in pairs,﴾ ﴿and made your sleep a rest,﴾ ﴿and made the night a covering,﴾ ﴿and made the day a time for livelihood,﴾ ﴿and built above you seven strong ones,﴾ ﴿and made a blazing lamp,﴾ ﴿and sent down from the rain-laden clouds abundant pouring water,﴾ ﴿that We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation,﴾ ﴿and gardens of thick growth.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Concerning what are they asking one another? About the great tidings﴾ means: about what are the polytheists asking one another? Because when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, Quraysh began to dispute and argue about what he called to.

Regarding "the great tidings" there are four opinions:
First: it is the Qur'an, said by Mujahid.
Second: it is the Day of Resurrection, said by Ibn Zayd.
Third: it is resurrection after death, said by Qatadah.
Fourth: it is about the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p. 183)

﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾ refers to resurrection, for death itself they did not dispute. On this there are two views:
One: the polytheists disagreed about it, some affirming and some denying, said by Qatadah.
Second: the Muslims and the polytheists disagreed about it, the Muslims affirming it and the polytheists denying it, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Regarding ﴿No! They will come to know﴾ and ﴿Again, no! They will come to know﴾ there are two views:
One: it is a threat following another threat to the disbelievers, said by al-Hasan. The first means: they will come to know the punishment that will befall them on the Day of Resurrection, and the second means: they will come to know the punishment that will befall them in Hell.
The second view: the first is for the disbelievers regarding the punishment they will receive in the Fire, and the second is for the believers regarding the reward they will receive in Paradise, said by al-Dahhak.

Regarding ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ there are four interpretations:
One: slumber, said by al-Suddi.
Second: tranquility, said by Qatadah.
Third: ease and repose, and for this reason Saturday was named "Sabt" because it is a day of ease and repose. Abu Ja'far al-Tabari said: it is said "sabata al-rajul" when a man rested.
Fourth: "subatan" means cutting off their works, because the root meaning of sabat is cutting, and from it comes the saying "sabata al-rajul sha'rahu" when he cut his hair. Al-Anbari said: Saturday was named so because work is cut off on it.

It may also carry a fifth meaning: that sabat is the state in which the senses are at rest so that one does not perceive through them.

Regarding ﴿And We made the night a covering﴾ there are two views:
One: tranquility, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi.
Second: a cover, because it covers its darkness as a garment covers the one who wears it, said by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

Regarding ﴿And We made the day a time for livelihood﴾ it means a time of earning, and it is called "ma'ash" because one lives by it.

(p. 184)

It may secondly mean: it is a time of living and pleasure.

Regarding ﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾ it means the sun by the lamp. Regarding "wahhaj" (blazing) there are four opinions:
One: shining, said by Ibn Abbas.
Second: sparkling, said by Mujahid.
Third: that it is from the heat of scorching, said by al-Hasan.
Fourth: that it is the burning one, which combines light and beauty.

Regarding ﴿And We sent down from the rain-laden clouds abundant pouring water﴾ there are three aspects:
One: "al-mu'sirat" (the rain-laden) are the winds, said by Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are the south winds.
Second: they are the clouds, said by Sufyan and al-Rabi'.
Third: "al-mu'sirat" is the sky, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Regarding "thajjaj" (abundant, pouring) there are two views:
One: it means abundant, said by Ibn Zayd.
Second: it means pouring forth, said by Ibn Abbas. Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

"So its top split open, then its bottom quaked, and it grew strait with the burden of water, pouring forth."

Regarding ﴿that We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation﴾ there are two views:
One: "habb" is what is in the husks of the crop that is harvested, and "nabat" is the herbage that is grazed. This is the meaning of al-Dahhak's view.
Second: "habb" is pearls, and "nabat" is grass. Ikrimah said: God does not send down a single drop from the sky without its causing a blade of grass to grow on the earth or a pearl in the sea.

It may thirdly mean: "habb" is what the sons of Adam sow, and "nabat" is what they did not sow.

Regarding ﴿and gardens of thick growth﴾ there are three aspects:
One: they are crops growing densely, side by side, said by Ikrimah.
Second: they are trees intertwined with fruit, said by al-Suddi.
Third: they are of various colors, said by al-Kalbi.

(p. 185)

It may fourthly mean: they are the lands whose surfaces are covered by crops and whose high places are covered by trees, so that crops and trees come together, intertwined.

The Day of Judgement is the Day of Decision (al-Fasl), meaning the Day of Resurrection. It is so called because on it the Judge will decide between the first and the last generations, and between those who are rewarded and those who are punished.

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾. In this there are two views:

First: an appointed meeting for gathering.

Second: a time for reward and punishment.

﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾. In this there are two views:

First: "they were set in motion" means they were removed from their places.

Second: they were blown away from their roots.

﴿And they became a mirage﴾. In this there are two views:

First: they became dust scattered (habā'an).

Second: they became like a mirage, from which nothing is obtained, like one who sees a mirage and thinks it is water, when it is not water.

﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying-in-wait (mirṣādan)﴾. In this there are three sayings:

The first: it means that it is watching, and so it will seize them for their deeds. This was said by Abu Sinan.

The second: that there is a watch-post over the Fire, and no one enters Paradise until he has passed over it. Whoever comes with a pass (jawāz) passes, and whoever does not come with a pass does not pass. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: that the mirṣād is a threat which Allah has threatened the disbelievers with. This was said by Qatadah.(p-186)

﴿For the tyrants, a place of return﴾. In this there are two sayings:

The first: a destination and a place of return. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: a refuge and a dwelling. This was said by Qatadah.

By "the tyrants" (al-ṭāghīn) is meant those who transgressed in their religion through disbelief, or in their worldly life through wrongdoing.

﴿Abiding therein for ages (aḥqāban)﴾. This means that whenever one age (ḥiqb) passes, another age comes, and so on forever. The scholars differed over the length of an ḥiqb, in seven sayings:

The first: eighty years. This was said by Abu Hurayrah.

The second: forty years. This was said by Ibn Umar.

The third: seventy years. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: it is a thousand months. This was narrated by Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fifth: three hundred years. This was said by Bashir ibn Ka'b.

The sixth: seventy thousand years. This was said by al-Hasan.

The seventh: it is a long period of time without limit. This was said by Qutrub.

Regarding the linking of their staying to the ages, there are two sayings:

The first: it is by way of multiplication: whenever ages pass, other ages come after them, and this is not a limit to their abiding in the Fire.

The second: that this is a limit to their punishment by the boiling water (ḥamīm) and the ghassāq; when the ages have ended, they will be punished with other kinds of punishment.

﴿They will not taste therein any coolness (bard) or any drink﴾. Regarding "coolness" (bard) there are three sayings:(p-187)

The first: that it is the coolness of water and the coolness of air. This is the view of many exegetes.

The second: that it is rest (rāḥah). This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that it is sleep. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu Ubaydah.

He cited the verse of al-Kindi:

Its sips grew cold upon me, so cold turned me away from them and from kissing them.

He means sleep.

"Drink" here means punishment.

It may also be that by "drink" is meant quenching of thirst, because drink quenches, whereas they will be thirsty forever therein.

﴿Except boiling water and ghassāq﴾. As for ḥamīm (boiling water), there are three sayings: The first: that it is the scorching heat that burns. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: the tears of their eyes in the Fire, which gather in pools within the Fire, and they are given them to drink. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that it is a kind of drink for the people of the Fire. This was said by al-Suddi.

As for ghassāq, there are four sayings: The first: that it is thick pus. This was said by Ibn Umar.

The second: that it is the cold, bitter freezing cold which burns from its coldness. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it is the pus of the people of the Fire. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: that it is foul-smelling in the dialect of al-Ṭaḥāwiyya. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿As a fitting recompense﴾. It is the plural of waqf (fitting); the people of ta'wil (interpretation) said: the evil recompense matched the evil deed.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: they did not expect reward, nor did they fear punishment. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they did not fear the threat of Allah concerning their reckoning and their recompense. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

The first: that it is much lying.

The second: that it is the denial of some of them by others. From this is the saying of the poet:

I believed her and I disbelieved her, and a man benefits from his lying.

This is a Yemeni dialect.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 78, verses 31–36:

﴿Indeed, for the righteous there is a place of success (mafaz).﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

The first: it means deliverance from its harms; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they succeeded in that they were saved from the Fire by Paradise, and from punishment by mercy; this is the view of Qatadah. The reality of this interpretation is that it is deliverance from destruction, and for this reason the desert when its water is scarce is called mafazah, as an optimistic omen of escape from it.

﴿And maidens of equal age (kawaʿib atraban).﴾ Regarding "kawaʿib" there are two views:

The first: the full-breasted, this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: virgins, this is the view of al-Dahhak, and from it is the verse of Qays ibn ʿAsim:

"And how many a noble woman, a chaste one, have we possessed, and how many a maiden who knew not the hardship of poverty, a girl of marriageable age."

Regarding "atraban" there are four views: The first: peers, this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: similar ones, this is the view of Mujahid.

The third: those who are mutually sincere (al-mutasafiyat), this is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The fourth: those who are mutually affectionate (al-mutaakhiyat), this is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿And a full cup (kasan dihaqan).﴾ Regarding it there are three views: The first: filled, this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, and from it is the words of the poet:

"ʿAmir came to us seeking hospitality, so we filled for him a full cup."

The second: successive, one following another, this is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The third: clear, transmitted by ʿUmar ibn ʿAta', and the poet said:

"You are dearer to the heart, nearer to the thirsty one than a full cup."

﴿They hear therein no idle talk (laghw) nor lying (kidhdhaban).﴾ Regarding "laghw" here there are four views: The first: falsehood, this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: swearing oaths when drinking it, this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: abuse, this is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: disobedience, this is the view of al-Hasan.

Regarding "kidhdhaban" there are three views: The first: that they do not call one another liars, this is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: that it is contention, this is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: that it is sin, this is the view of Qatadah.

Regarding His words "They hear therein" there are two views:

The first: in Paradise, this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: in drinking wine, this is the view of Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿A recompense from your Lord, a gift reckoned (ʿataʾan hisaban).﴾ Regarding it there are three views: The first: sufficient, this is the view of al-Kalbi.

The second: abundant, this is the view of Qatadah.

The third: a reckoning for what they did, so "hisab" here means counting.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 78, verses 37–40:

﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks﴾. Regarding "the Spirit" here there are eight opinions. The first: the Spirit is a creation of God's creation, in the likeness of people, but they are not humans; they are an army of God, glory be to Him. This was said by Abu Salih.

The second: they are the most noble of the angels. This was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The third: they are guardians over the angels. This was said by Ibn Abi Najih.

The third: they are guardians over the angels in creation. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: it is an angel, one of the greatest of the angels in creation. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: it is Jibril, peace be upon him. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: they are the children of Adam. This was said by Qatadah.

The seventh: they are the children of Adam. This was said by Qatadah.

The eighth: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

﴿They will not speak except those whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: they will not intercede except for those whom the Most Merciful has permitted to intercede. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: they will not speak about anything except that which the Most Merciful has permitted, namely the testimony that there is no god but God. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿And he speaks what is right﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: it means what is true. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: it is the statement "There is no god but God." This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: the Spirit will say on the Day of Resurrection: "No one enters Paradise except by mercy, and no one enters the Fire except by deeds." This is the meaning of His words ﴿and he speaks what is right﴾. This was said by al-Hasan.

It may also admit a fourth meaning: that it is the question of the seeker and the answer of the one sought, because the speech of creation on the Day of Resurrection is restricted to question and answer.

﴿That is the true Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. Regarding its being called "the true" there are two explanations:

One: because its coming is true, while they had been in doubt.

The second: because God, exalted is He, judges in it with truth, by reward and punishment.

﴿Whoever wills, let him take a path to his Lord as a place of return﴾. Regarding this there are two explanations:

One: "a path." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: "a place of return." This was said by Ibn Isa.

It may also admit a third: he takes a reward by his deeds deserved, because the place of return is due to both the believer and the disbeliever.

﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾. Regarding this there are two explanations:

One: the punishment of this world, because it is the nearer of the two punishments. This was said by Qatadah, and Muqatil said: it is the killing of the Quraysh at Badr.

The second: the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, because it is coming, and everything that is coming is near. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Kalbi.

﴿On the Day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forth﴾, meaning, on the Day when a man looks at what he has sent forth of good deeds. al-Hasan said: "He sent forth, so he arrives at what he sent forth."

It may also be that it is general: the believer's looking at what he sent forth of good, and the disbeliever's looking at what he sent forth of evil.

﴿And the disbeliever will say: "Oh, would that I were dust!"﴾ Mujahid said: The animals will be resurrected, and they will be brought to avenge the hornless one against the one with horns, and the one struck with hooves against the one who kicked, and the one gored against the one who gored. Then the Lord, exalted is He, will say: "Be dust," without Paradise or Fire. Then the disbeliever will say at that moment: "Oh, would that I were dust!" And regarding his saying that there are two explanations:

One: "Oh, would that I had become today like them, dust, without Paradise or Fire." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "Oh, would that I had been like this animal in the world, and that I were today dust." This was said by Abu Hurayrah. This is among the false wishes, as the poet said:

"Ah, would that I... though a man is dead, and wishing does not avail against the calamities of fate. Wish!"

Muqatil said: the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿On the Day when a man looks at what his hands have sent forth﴾ were revealed concerning Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi, and the words of God, exalted is He, ﴿And the disbeliever will say: "Oh, would that I were dust!"﴾ were revealed concerning his brother al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad.
